title: A Wind Tunnel in a Bicycle Shop

passage.title: A Wind Tunnel in a Bicycle Shop
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
In the autumn of 1901, Wilbur and Orville Wright returned to Dayton, Ohio, feeling discouraged. They had just spent weeks flying a full-sized glider on the sandy dunes of Kitty Hawk, North Carolina. Before building the glider, the brothers had used math tables printed by flight experts. Those tables told how much lift their cloth wings should produce. Out in the ocean breeze, however, the glider rose only a third as high as the printed charts promised. Wilbur began to suspect that the published air tables were flawed.

Testing new full-sized wings out on the windy coast took months of travel and repair. The brothers needed a way to test dozens of wing shapes right inside their bicycle workshop without waiting for good weather. First, they mounted a small wing and a flat plate onto the front wheel of a bicycle and pedaled fast down a Dayton street. Even that clever test told them that the old math charts were wrong. Still, street gusts were too uneven for exact measurements.

So the brothers built a six-foot wooden trough with a glass viewing window on top. At one end, a belt-driven fan pushed a fast stream of air through a metal honeycomb grid that smoothed out turbulent swirls. Inside the six-foot wooden box in their Dayton shop, miniature wing models cut from sheet steel were tested by Wilbur and Orville against a steady blast of fan air. Each model wing was no larger than a playing card.

To measure how each wing behaved, the brothers crafted two delicate balances out of old hacksaw blades and bicycle spokes. One balance measured lift, the upward force that holds an airplane in the sky. The other balance measured drag, the backward pull of air resistance. Peering through the top glass pane, Orville and Wilbur recorded the exact angle of the balances in notebooks.

Over two winter months, they tested more than two hundred miniature wings of different curves, widths, and thicknesses. Their precise notes proved that long, narrow wings with a gentle curve sliced through the air far better than stubby, thick ones. Armed with their own wind-tunnel data, the Wright brothers built their 1902 glider. It soared smoothly over the dunes and paved the way for the first powered airplane a year later.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 3:

"Inside the six-foot wooden box in their Dayton shop, miniature wing models cut from sheet steel were tested by Wilbur and Orville against a steady blast of fan air."

In this sentence, who or what actually performed the action of testing the miniature wing models?

options.text: The six-foot wooden box in the Dayton shop
Wilbur and Orville
The sheet steel cutting into the fan blades
Famous flight experts visiting from North Carolina

questions.provingSentenceText: Inside the six-foot wooden box in their Dayton shop, miniature wing models cut from sheet steel were tested by Wilbur and Orville against a steady blast of fan air.
questions.childTip: Find the passive verb 'were tested by' to see who conducted the experiment.
questions.parentExplanation: In this passive sentence, 'miniature wing models cut from sheet steel' is the receiver of the verb 'were tested.' The true actors appear right after the preposition 'by': 'Wilbur and Orville' (Option B).

questions.prompt:
Read these sentences from Paragraph 1:

"Out in the ocean breeze, however, the glider rose only a third as high as the printed charts promised. Wilbur began to suspect that the published air tables were flawed."

What does the word "flawed" mean as it is used in Paragraph 1?

options.text: Inaccurate and containing serious mistakes
Written in a secret code that only pilots could read
Completely proven by every glider flight at Kitty Hawk
Printed on heavy steel sheets instead of paper

questions.provingSentenceText: Wilbur began to suspect that the published air tables were flawed.
questions.childTip: Look at why Wilbur doubted the charts: the glider rose only a third as high as the charts promised.
questions.parentExplanation: Because the glider produced far less lift than the printed tables predicted—and Paragraph 2 confirms 'the old math charts were wrong'—'flawed' means inaccurate and containing mistakes (Option A).

questions.prompt: Why did the Wright brothers place a metal honeycomb grid at the front of their wooden wind tunnel?

options.text: To keep the sheet-steel wings from flying out of the box and hitting the glass window
To smooth out rough, swirling air from the fan so the wind flowed evenly past the models
To heat the air inside the bicycle shop during the cold Ohio winter months
To block all air from entering the wooden trough while Orville drew in his notebook

questions.provingSentenceText: At one end, a belt-driven fan pushed a fast stream of air through a metal honeycomb grid that smoothed out turbulent swirls.
questions.childTip: Click the sentence in Paragraph 3 that tells what the metal honeycomb grid did to the fan air.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 3 states that 'a belt-driven fan pushed a fast stream of air through a metal honeycomb grid that smoothed out turbulent swirls,' ensuring a steady, even airflow for accurate testing (Option B).

questions.prompt: PART A: What key discovery did the Wright brothers make by testing two hundred model wings in their wind tunnel?

options.text: Thick, stubby wings made of cloth rose three times higher than thin steel wings.
Famous flight experts had already tested every possible wing shape on a bicycle wheel.
Long, narrow wings with a gentle curve performed much better in the air than thick, stubby wings.
Gliders could fly without any wings at all if a belt-driven fan was bolted to the front.

questions.provingSentenceText: Their precise notes proved that long, narrow wings with a gentle curve sliced through the air far better than stubby, thick ones.
questions.childTip: Look in Paragraph 5 to see what their precise notes proved about the best wing shape.
questions.parentExplanation: Aligned to ELAGSE5RI1, Paragraph 5 explicitly states what their wind-tunnel notes proved: 'long, narrow wings with a gentle curve sliced through the air far better than stubby, thick ones' (Option C).
